period: July close, prepared from the QuickBooks Online general ledger, with June as the comparison month
caption: The twelve accounts the memo was written against.
threshold: A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
policyScope: The threshold sets what the monthly management report has to explain. It does not make a known error, or anything else that looks wrong, exempt from attention.
evidenceNote: Every sentence under On file is a verified case assumption. A fact that is not listed was not supplied, which is not the same as saying the firm has no such document. Where a sentence is not carried by the evidence, the case says it is not established from supplied evidence rather than calling it fabricated.
ledgerNote: The fifth element on each ledger row is 1 when the movement clears both legs of the threshold and 0 when it does not. index.html does not read it.
ledger: Hardware and licence cost of resale

cards.name: Software licences and hosting
cards.memo: Software licences and hosting rose $25,300 to $57,900 on the annual renewal of the monitoring platform, billed in July (source: vendor invoice).
file: No vendor invoice was supplied. The citation inside the sentence is the draft describing its own support.
Nothing on file states what period the monitoring platform renewal covers.
A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
cards.why: The account moved $35,300 and the sentence says $25,300, so the figure is $10,000 short of what the two columns produce and the reason is attached to a number the books do not carry. The renewal is not established from supplied evidence either, because no invoice was handed over and nothing on file says what period it covers, so a period defect is not established here and should not be claimed as one. Ask for the invoice and the term it covers, and the $10,000 gap will either belong to the renewal or to something else sitting in the account.
cards.truth: The account moved $35,300 and the sentence says $25,300, so the figure is $10,000 short of what the ledger produces.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for the monitoring platform invoice and the term it covers.
cards.tell: The memo handed you a number, so subtract the two columns yourself before you read the reason attached to it.

cards.name: Subcontracted engineering
cards.memo: Subcontracted engineering fell $46,500 to $88,300 as the cutover was staffed through two partner firms (source: partner invoices on file).
file: Travel and onsite delivery, account 5200, rose $26,500 over the same month.
No partner invoice summary was supplied, and nothing on file states how much of the $88,300 either partner firm billed.
A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
cards.why: The $46,500 ties and the word in front of it does not, because the account went from $41,800 to $88,300 and the sentence reads as a fall against a June balance that is lower than July's. Subcontracted engineering more than doubling in a month is the movement that needed explaining, and it is still unexplained: two partner firms may well have staffed the cutover, and no partner invoice summary was supplied, so how much of the $88,300 they billed is not established from supplied evidence.
cards.truth: The account rose $46,500 rather than falling, so the sentence has the movement backwards and the reason for a rise that size is still missing.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for a partner invoice summary for June and for July.
cards.tell: Read the direction word against the two columns, because a figure that ties can still sit next to the wrong verb.

cards.name: Client acquisition costs
cards.memo: Client acquisition costs rose $9,300, or 189.8 percent, which fails the dollar leg of the threshold, so this line carries no driver.
file: A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
The threshold sets what the monthly management report has to explain. It does not make a known error, or anything else that looks wrong, exempt from attention.
cards.why: The dollar figure ties, the percentage ties, and $9,300 never reaches $25,000, so both legs are not met and the reporting policy asks for nothing on this line. The memo reads the threshold correctly and declines to invent a cause, which is the right answer on a movement this size.
cards.over: One hundred and ninety percent is the largest percentage on the statement and it sits on the smallest dollar movement on it, and the dollar leg is the one that decides the line.
cards.tell: A big percentage of a small balance is still a small number, and saying that a line owes nothing is a correct answer.

cards.name: Project and implementation revenue
cards.memo: Project and implementation revenue rose $57.5k to $96,400, up 147.8 percent, on the Riverbend cutover that ran the whole month (source: project billing schedule).
file: No project billing schedule was supplied. The citation inside the sentence is the draft describing its own support.
Kestrel bills project work to eleven clients and the ledger is not broken out by client.

Travel and onsite delivery, account 5200, carries $26,500 of approved Riverbend onsite costs in July, which places cutover work in the month and says nothing about how much revenue that work produced.
Nothing on file states the Riverbend contract value, the milestone amounts, or which clients the $96,400 came from.
cards.why: The dollar figure ties and the percentage ties, so arithmetic is not what fails here. Nothing supplied connects the Riverbend cutover to the $57,500, because the schedule the sentence names was never handed over and the ledger does not split project revenue by client, so the driver is not established from supplied evidence, which is a smaller claim than saying it is false. The travel account shows cutover work happening in July, and that is context rather than proof of the amount. A project billing schedule by client and milestone for both months would settle it.
cards.truth: Nothing supplied connects the Riverbend cutover to the $57,500, because the billing schedule the sentence cites was never supplied.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for a project billing schedule by client and milestone for June and for July.
cards.tell: A source named inside the draft is not a source on file, so ask which document was actually handed over.

cards.name: Salaries and wages
cards.memo: Salaries and wages held flat at $88,500, with no headcount movement in the month (source: payroll register).
file: The June and July payroll registers are on file. Gross pay is $88,500 in each month, the same twenty-two employees appear on both, and no pay rate changed.
Nothing was charged to overtime or to a bonus accrual in July, and the registers carry base pay only.
A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
cards.why: The account did not move at all, so neither leg of the threshold is close and the policy asks for nothing here. The sentence goes further than the policy requires and the registers on file carry it from end to end, with the same twenty-two people at the same rates in both months and no overtime or bonus accrual behind the figure.
cards.over: Nothing moved on this line in a month when the rest of the statement moved a great deal, and that is what pulls a reviewer in. The registers on file answer it, and a line that did not move owed no commentary in the first place.
cards.tell: The sentence names the payroll register and the register is genuinely on file, which is the difference between this line and the three sentences that cite a document nobody supplied.

cards.name: Hardware and licence resale
cards.memo: Hardware and licence resale came down $52,000 to $96,000 as the two largest clients finished their refresh cycles, and July is the run rate to expect from here.
file: From 1 July, Kestrel moved its two largest clients off resold perpetual licences and onto a bundled subscription billed inside recurring managed services on account 4000 (client pricing memo of 12 June on file).
Recurring managed services, account 4000, rose $36,900 over the same month.
No resale billing bridge by client was supplied, so the gross movement behind the $52,000 net fall is not known.
No sentence in the memo connects the two revenue lines to each other.
cards.why: From 1 July the licence spend of the two largest clients is billed inside recurring managed services rather than on this account, and the memo never mentions the change, so calling the fall a finished refresh cycle is not established from supplied evidence. How much of the $52,000 is that reclassification is not established either, because $52,000 is the net fall and other resale billings could have moved in either direction underneath it. The forecast sentence carries nothing behind it at all, and the ask is a resale billing bridge by client rather than a cause you supply yourself.
cards.truth: From 1 July the two largest clients are billed inside recurring managed services rather than on this account, and the memo never mentions the change.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for a resale billing bridge on account 4200 by client.
cards.tell: When one revenue line falls while a related one rises, ask whether anything moved between them, and ask for the bridge rather than reading the net fall as the amount that moved.

cards.name: Hardware and licence cost of resale
cards.memo: Hardware and licence cost of resale fell $35,400 to $65,300 with the resale billings it supports, and the resale gross margin held at 32.0 percent in June and in July.
file: Resale gross margin is account 4200 less account 5100, divided by account 4200.
Account 4200 ran $148,000 in June and $96,000 in July. Account 5100 ran $100,700 and $65,300.
The vendor cost report on file matches every July resale cost line to a resale invoice and reconciles the $65,300 to July resale billings of $96,000.
A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
cards.why: Recompute it and the margin holds, because $47,300 on $148,000 is 32.0 percent and $30,700 on $96,000 is 32.0 percent, so the cost came down in step with the billings rather than ahead of them. The vendor cost report on file ties the whole $65,300 to July resale invoices, so the cause is carried by a document instead of asserted. The sentence says what this cost did and does not claim to know why the billings fell, and that second question is the one sitting on account 4200.
cards.over: One event sits behind this line and behind account 4200, and only one of the two sentences is supported. This one keeps to what the cost report covers.
cards.tell: Recompute the ratio before you decide a cost moved on its own, and read what the sentence actually claims rather than what the line beside it claims.

cards.name: Project and implementation revenue
cards.memo: Project and implementation revenue carries the final Riverbend milestone, which was billed on 31 July and accepted the same day (source: signed acceptance certificate).
file: A signed acceptance certificate for the final Riverbend milestone is on file. It is dated 4 August 2026 and records acceptance on 4 August.
The milestone invoice sits in the 31 July billing run.
Nothing on file states how much of the milestone work was performed by 31 July, and no contract extract stating what acceptance is for was supplied.
Kestrel closes on the fifth business day of the following month.
cards.why: The one document on file contradicts the sentence, because the certificate is dated 4 August and records acceptance on 4 August while the memo places acceptance on 31 July. The billing date is not in dispute and it is not what settles the period either. What is missing is how much of the milestone work was performed by 31 July and what the contract makes acceptance do, so the amount of milestone revenue that belongs in July is an open question rather than a proved error.
cards.truth: The acceptance certificate on file is dated 4 August and records acceptance on 4 August, so the fact the sentence rests on falls in the next period.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for the milestone billing detail, the contract clause on acceptance, and what portion of the work was performed by 31 July.
cards.tell: A document on file is not the same as a document that says what the memo says it says, so check its date before you accept the sentence built on it.

cards.name: Insurance, cyber liability included
cards.memo: Insurance rose $2,700 to $9,600 on the cyber liability renewal that took effect 1 July, and the movement fails the dollar leg of the threshold.
file: The broker's renewal schedule on file shows the cyber liability charge rising from $2,400 a month to $5,100 a month from 1 July.
The rest of the account is general liability and errors and omissions at $4,500 a month, unchanged in both months.
The annual premium is carried in prepaid insurance and released monthly, and the July prepaid schedule on file agrees to the $9,600.
A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
cards.why: The renewal schedule and the prepaid schedule on file account for every dollar, because $4,500 of unchanged cover plus $5,100 of cyber liability is July's $9,600, and the $2,400 the cyber cover cost in June is the whole of the $2,700 movement. The threshold reading is right as well, since $2,700 never reaches $25,000, so the memo explained a line it did not have to explain and got it right.
cards.over: An annual renewal landing in one month is usually where a whole premium gets charged to a single period, and the prepaid schedule on file closes that door here.
cards.tell: A cause carried by a document on file holds, whatever the percentage looks like.

cards.name: Computer equipment
cards.memo: Computer equipment of $21,900 carries the network core refresh, bought outright and expensed in July, and the movement fails the dollar leg of the threshold.
file: The vendor invoice on file lists six rack servers at $2,900 each and two core switches at $2,250 each, all placed in service on 20 July.
Kestrel capitalises any single item costing more than $2,000 and depreciates it over its useful life (fixed asset policy on file).
June's $3,200 in this account is peripherals, none of them over $2,000.
Depreciation, account 7000, was $6,200 in June and $6,200 in July, and nothing was added to the fixed asset register in July.
The threshold sets what the monthly management report has to explain. It does not make a known error, or anything else that looks wrong, exempt from attention.
cards.why: Every one of the eight items on the invoice costs more than $2,000, so the firm's own capitalisation policy puts all $21,900 in fixed assets rather than in an expense account, and the depreciation charge sitting unchanged at $6,200 shows that nothing was capitalised. The threshold reading in the sentence is correct and it settles nothing, because the policy decides what the management report must explain and does not put a known misposting beyond attention.
cards.truth: Every item on the invoice clears the $2,000 capitalisation policy, so the $21,900 belongs in fixed assets, and depreciation did not move because nothing was capitalised.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for the fixed asset addition schedule and the July depreciation calculation.
cards.tell: A line can owe no commentary and still sit in the wrong account, so read the invoice against the capitalisation policy.

cards.name: Travel and onsite delivery
cards.memo: Travel and onsite delivery rose $26,500 to $32,900 on the onsite weeks the Riverbend cutover ran in July.
file: The approved July expense report file is on file. It codes $26,500 of lodging, airfare and mileage above June's level to the Riverbend cutover, and every item in it is dated in July.
June carried no onsite project work, and its $6,400 is recurring local mileage that continues unchanged in July.
The expense report file covers what the cutover cost and states nothing about what the cutover billed.
A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
cards.why: The movement clears both legs, so this line owes commentary, and the commentary it owes is the commentary it received. The approved expense file codes the whole $26,500 to the cutover and the recurring $6,400 of local mileage is unchanged, so the two together are July's $32,900 and the cause is carried by a document rather than asserted. That is what separates this sentence from the revenue sentence resting on the same cutover.
cards.over: The cutover is the weakest claim in the memo on the revenue side, and that does not make every sentence mentioning it weak. The expense file carries this one, for the cost and for nothing else.
cards.tell: Ask which document would prove the sentence, and here the approved expense file does.

cards.name: Recurring managed services
file: A line owes commentary only when it clears both $25,000 and 10 percent.
No sentence in the memo touches this account.
From 1 July the two largest clients are billed a bundled subscription on this account that includes licence spend previously resold on account 4200 (client pricing memo of 12 June on file).
No client count, no contract schedule and no revenue bridge by client was supplied for June or for July.
cards.why: The account moved $36,900 and 22.8 percent, which clears both legs with room to spare, and the memo reaches the reviewer with nothing written against the largest recurring line in the business. The pricing change on file makes at least part of the rise a reclassification out of resale rather than new work, and how much is not established from supplied evidence, because no revenue bridge by client was handed over. Ask for the bridge rather than reading the movement as growth.
cards.truth: $36,900 is 22.8 percent and clears both legs, and the memo says nothing about this line at all.
cards.ask: Ask the controller for a revenue bridge on account 4000 by client for June and for July.
cards.tell: Read the ledger for what the memo left out, not only for what it got wrong.

basisKeyNote: basisKey is the set of basis chips that are correct for the card. A chip outside that set contradicts the key for this card. The reason is scored right when the player chose at least one chip in the key and no chip outside it. A card whose key is 'stand' carries only "the figure and reason hold", because a chip naming a defect contradicts a line that has none. The reason score is a compatibility check on the stated basis, not a rubric score; the three-dimension reasoning rubric is scored by a person outside the page.

changeLog.changed: First release. Twelve accounts and twelve lines, keyed seven flags and five stands, covering arithmetic, wrong direction, unsupported driver, unsupported attribution, wrong account, timing, no explanation and the clean line.
changeLog.why: Halyard is the only practice case and it runs on distribution. A managed IT services firm gives the drill a second industry with a different chart of accounts and a different set of traps.

changeLog.changed: The six accounts and six memo sentences in the checker.html Kestrel sample are carried over unchanged: 4000, 4100 with two sentences, 5000, 6000, 6200 and 6400. Their figures and the calls they imply are the same in both places.
changeLog.why: The checker sample and this case are the same memo, so a verdict reached in one has to hold in the other. Six accounts were added around them, 4200, 5100, 5200, 6300, 6500 and 7000, with a total revenue, cost of sales, operating expense and net line that reconcile.

changeLog.changed: The comparison columns are June and July, carried in a new columns field, and not May and June.
changeLog.why: The checker sample is titled July 2026 compared with June 2026, and keeping the figures consistent with it means keeping its months. index.html prints the column headers May and June as literals, so the lane that wires case selection has to read columns from the case file.

changeLog.changed: Card 10, computer equipment, is the first card in any case whose basisKey is "wrong account".
changeLog.why: cases/README.md recorded that no card in the release had an amount booked in an account it does not belong in, so tapping that chip scored zero everywhere. This case gives the chip one line where it is right.

changeLog.changed: Four sentences cite a source inside the draft. Three of those documents were never supplied and one of them, the payroll register on card 5, is genuinely on file.
changeLog.why: A draft's assertion about its own support is not independent evidence, and a case that made every cited source missing would teach a shortcut instead of the distinction.
